"In the sweltering heat of a Darwin night, the air thick with the scent of frangipani and the distant hum of cicadas, Dale Scott Walkinshaw stumbled through the shadows, his mind a whirlwind of alcohol and adrenaline. The crash had been a blur—one moment he was laughing, the next, metal screamed against wood as his Toyota Hilux plowed into a palm tree. The impact had jolted him back to reality, but the world still spun, his vision swimming as he fumbled for the door.

His passenger, a young woman whose name he barely knew, groaned in his arms, her breath shallow. She had been vibrant just hours before, her laughter ringing through the bar as they shared drinks, her hand brushing his in a fleeting moment of connection. Now, her skin was pale, her body limp, and Dale’s heart pounded with a mix of panic and guilt. He had promised to get her home safe. Instead, he had driven them both into disaster.

Sirens wailed in the distance, growing louder. Dale’s pulse quickened. He knew the drill—police, questions, the cold bite of handcuffs. He had been here before, in the back of a caged van, the metal bars pressing into his skin as he raged against the walls, his voice raw with desperation. The memory of those moments clawed at him, the suffocating darkness, the way no one had heard him until it was almost too late.

Two officers approached, their flashlights cutting through the night. One knelt beside the woman, radioing for an ambulance, while the other turned to Dale, his expression unreadable. ‘You’re under arrest,’ the officer said, his voice flat. Dale didn’t resist. He knew the routine. But as the cuffs clicked around his wrists, a cold dread settled in his stomach. The van was waiting. And this time, he wasn’t sure he’d make it out alive.

The ride to the station was a blur of motion and noise—the rumble of the engine, the occasional crackle of the radio, the officer in the front seat glancing back at him with something like pity. Dale pressed his forehead against the bars, his breath fogging the metal. He thought of the coroner’s words, the damning report about the lack of cameras, the ignored warnings. *It wasn’t a matter of if a person would die in the back of a police van but when.*

The van hit a bump, jolting him. His chest tightened. He could feel the walls closing in, the air growing thinner. He thought of the woman in the car, her life hanging in the balance, and wondered if his would end here, in the dark, where no one would see. The officer in the passenger seat turned, his eyes meeting Dale’s for a brief, unreadable moment. Then he looked away.

Dale closed his eyes. Somewhere in the distance, a siren faded into the night. And in the back of the van, the silence stretched on, heavy with the weight of all the things left unsaid."
